title: Not Everyone Needs College, But They Do Need to Learn to Read
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler argues that the growth of skilled-trades and middle-skill pathways does not remove the need for strong literacy, because many high school graduates cannot read well enough to benefit from even brief vocational programs. She uses a practice GED question, reports on students pushed through high school unable to read, and cites national data showing that 30 percent of twelfth graders score below Basic, disproportionately Black, Hispanic and lower-income. Technical documents and manuals demand fluency, sophisticated vocabulary and complex syntax, which schools fail to build through content-rich curriculum from the early grades. She holds that the problem is instructional rather than innate, since evidence-based methods could teach about 95 percent of children to decode. Her remedy is to fix K-12 reading instruction with systematic phonics combined with knowledge and vocabulary building.
points: Skilled-trades jobs are growing, but they still require fluent reading of manuals and technical documents, so literacy is a prerequisite for non-college pathways too.
Persistent reading failure is a teaching problem, not a student ability problem, because scientifically supported methods could teach roughly 95 percent of children to decode.
High school teachers are generally not trained to teach basic reading skills, so students who arrive without fluency rarely get help.
Vocabulary gaps are hard to predict and arise from schools not systematically building knowledge through content-rich curriculum from the early grades.
The long-term fix is universal adoption of curricula that pair systematic phonics with knowledge and vocabulary building, with listening supports and adult phonics instruction as stopgaps.
quotes: Manufacturing jobs—the kind that require only a high school diploma but still pay a living wage—have been disappearing fast, despite promises to save them. At the same time, other kinds of jobs are on the increase: ones that pay well and require something more than high school but less than a bachelor’s degree. In 2018, it was estimated that there would be 16 million such openings by 2024, most of them paying more than $55,000 a year, and many paying more than $80,000.

In another indication of the extent of the problem, a former D.C. teacher I know tested all 150 9th graders at a high-poverty school some years ago and found that the average reading level was 3rd grade. High school teachers haven’t been trained to teach basic reading skills, so these students rarely get the help they need.

Even students who have the basics down often can’t decipher words easily enough to achieve reading “fluency,” which is a key factor in comprehension. On national reading tests, 30% of 12th graders score below the “Basic” category, which translates into about 1.35 million students.
It’s not that these students can’t learn to read. If schools used methods supported by scientific evidence, it’s been estimated that 95% of all children could learn to read or “decode” words.

Again, it’s not that these students couldn’t have learned these words. The problem is that schools fail to systematically build knowledge of this kind of vocabulary through content-rich curriculum beginning in the early grades, diving deeply into topics so that kids have the context that will enable them to absorb and retain the words’ meaning.

The long-term solution is to fix our K-12 education system so that it’s no longer turning out so many teenagers and adults who struggling with reading. Unfortunately, the effects of the pandemic are making that dire situation even worse.

The better news is that an increasing number of schools and districts are adopting curricula that provide children with systematic instruction in phonics while simultaneously building sophisticated vocabulary. If we want all students to have a decent chance of success in life—with or without college—we need to do whatever we can to make that approach universal.
